title: At the feast of Dedication (John 10:22–42)
hook: in winter, at Hanukkah in Solomon's porch, they ask him plainly

segments.voice: Yesterday, a painting in the catacombs, and the good shepherd, unlike the hireling, who knows his sheep. Your line was I know my own. Whose name did you learn or use? Day six hundred twenty-one.

"And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter." Two little facts, and they set a whole scene. The feast of the dedication is Hanukkah. The feast's own story is told in First Maccabees, a book that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include. And it's winter, cold enough that Jesus is walking under cover, in the colonnade called Solomon's porch. A crowd gathers around him there, close, maybe blocking his way. And they ask the question that has followed him for chapters.

First, the feast. Long before Jesus, a Greek king named Antiochus the Fourth set up pagan worship in the temple in Jerusalem and tried to stamp out Jewish practice. A family called the Maccabees led a revolt. When they took back the temple, they cleansed it and dedicated it again, with an eight-day celebration. The book of First Maccabees describes it. Hanukkah means dedication. The famous story of a small jar of oil burning for eight days is told later, in the Talmud. Jews keep Hanukkah to this day, lighting lights in winter. So here is Jesus, at the feast that remembers the temple made holy again. And the crowd says: "How long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly." His answer: I've told you, and the works I do tell you. My sheep hear my voice. Then a promise: "And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." Pluck is the King James word. Some modern Bibles say snatch, like a wolf grabbing a lamb. And then he goes further: no one can pluck them out of my Father's hand. "I and my Father are one." The crowd hears it as blasphemy and picks up stones again. He escapes across the Jordan, to the place where John baptized at the very start. And there, John says, many believed. The story circles back to where it began.
screen: then, large: `I AND MY FATHER ARE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a light for the winter. If there's a candle or lamp nearby, light it or switch it on. If not, picture one. Settle, and breathe. Watch the light for a moment. Think of someone going through a winter right now: grief, illness, loneliness, fear. Picture them held safe, in hands that won't let go. Then think of your own winter, if you're in one. If you pray, you can hold that person, and yourself, in the promise that no one can snatch them away. If you don't, simply keep the light company. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. The Jewish feast of the dedication, remembering the temple cleansed and dedicated again. Jesus walked in the temple at Hanukkah, in winter.
Your line: no one can snatch them. Today, send one message to the person in a winter you thought of, so they know they're held. Day six hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight nights each winter, lighting one more light each night; Christians read this passage as Jesus's plain claim of unity with the Father and a promise that his own are held safe.

notes: 'Only time Hanukkah is mentioned in the Bible's sixty-six books as Protestants count them': First Maccabees (in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles) and 2 Maccabees describe its origin. Confirm phrasing.
Rededication date about 164 BC under Judas Maccabeus after Antiochus IV Epiphanes's desecration (167 BC); 'about two centuries before Jesus'. Confirm.
Oil miracle first told in the Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 21b. Confirm.
Solomon's porch on the temple's east side (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.7). Confirm.
Index carry 'snatch'; KJV 'pluck'. Script explains both.
The Jewish neighbor reference is descriptive, with no comparison. Confirm.
